2026-08-21.headline: Score HOLDS at 27/30 for an eleventh consecutive edition. No channel moved. The buyback rally lasted exactly one session, and what took it back was American economic data rather than anything that happened in the Gulf. On Thursday 20 August the 30-year rose 5.65 bp to 5.2476%, giving back 62% of Wednesday’s 9.15 bp fall and leaving the tenor 5.84 bp below Monday’s war high; the 10-year rose 5.75 bp to 4.7041%; the dollar’s three-month low lasted a single close. Stage-4 Threshold B RE-ARMED on the very next close — the fifth arming and the ninth state since 29 July, and the THIRD time in this war that B has re-armed after exactly one session out, after 10 and 14 August. The standing warning that a single long-end session does not survive contact with the next one is now vindicated five times over and should be read as the governing rule rather than as a caveat. The cause is on the tape and it is domestic: the Philadelphia Fed’s August manufacturing index printed +47.4, which the Bank reports as a five-year high, initial claims came in at 206,000, existing home sales beat at 4.05M and the leading index’s six-month growth rate turned positive. A long end that fell 9 bp on a buyback announcement gave most of it back to a single strong American data day, which tells you what the buyback actually bought: a level, not a regime. Second, and it is the reconciliation that carries it: the Singapore snapshot understated every reconciled field bar one, all the same way, for the second time this month. Brent settled $1.92 above the print carried here on Thursday morning, and the curve settled 2.75 to 6.74 bp above it across the 2- to 30-year. Three readings the last edition took from that snapshot are withdrawn as TRENDS, not as facts about the 19 August close, which is unrestated and whose superlatives all hold: that Threshold B’s lapse would persist, that the two legs of the Treasury downgrade were converging, and that the dollar had established a durable three-month low. Third, European gas took out its war-record CLOSE for the first time since 24 July. TTF closed €65.295, above the €63.649 record close of 24 July, after two consecutive editions in which only the intraday print cleared it. It is now 109.1% above its pre-war level while US Henry Hub sits 10.8% BELOW its own — the cleanest single pair of numbers in this document for the proposition that this is a Hormuz routing dislocation and not a global energy shock. Fourth, oil keeps closing in, and it is still the only live scoring question here. Brent closed $91.97 on the scored continuation, the highest since 24 July and a fifth consecutive up-close; the active contract closed $93.78, the highest since 23 July. The upgrade sits $3.03 away on the scored series and $1.22 on the active close — a fourth consecutive edition of narrowing. Read the roll disclosure in the oil-channel analysis before treating either figure as a record proximity. Fifth, Washington moved from blockade to declared economic war, and Tehran answered by pointing at the American bond market. Trump announced an “ECONOMIC D-DAY” late on 19 August, after the last edition’s Singapore cut, and Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC on 20 August that it is “a one-two punch… we are going to collapse this regime” and that on third countries “you’re either with us or against us”, declining to say whether China would be targeted. Foreign Minister Araghchi’s reply the same day called it “a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt and surging interest costs”. That is a foreign minister naming the transmission channel this document exists to measure. And the sanctions that landed are not the sanctions that were trailed: OFAC did act on 20 August, but on a Hizballah cash-smuggling network with three IRGC-Qods Force-linked designees — no oil, no shipping, no ship registries, no exchange houses. Sixth, the frozen physical record broke. UKMTO published Update 087 on 20 August: the cumulative count moves 91 → 94 on three new incidents, and the document’s own language changes — 086 said attack frequency “has increased”, 087 says it “has remained consistent… and the environment reflects an established post-MoU status quo”. The blockade tally moves to 65 redirected as of 19 August. Against that, CENTCOM’s combat silence inside Iran reaches 23 days, and the one thing it announced on 20 August — through press rather than its own releases index, and so Tier 2 — was the arrival of the USS George Washington. Sequencing 27 → 27 → 27.

The three new incidents — 116-26, 117-26, 118-26

116-26 (logged 18 Aug) — ATTACK, STRAIT OF HORMUZ. A bulk carrier, name withheld; OSINT reported a vessel attacked on 15 August, and a nearby vessel relayed VHF contact with the Master, who stated that a rocket hit the starboard side under the gangway, with one confirmed crew fatality. Vessel not under command; no environmental damage. 117-26 (18 Aug) — ATTACK, BAB EL-MANDEB. Six anti-ship ballistic missiles were fired at an anchored vessel in Yemeni territorial waters and five struck, causing complete structural destruction; no crew and no cargo were aboard. 118-26 (20 Aug) — HIJACK, GULF OF ADEN, the tanker SEAMULL (a.k.a. SIBU 1), Eritrea-flagged, 34NM off Yemen in the eastern IRTC; upgraded from attack to hijack at 0957Z with about six armed persons aboard stating an intent to proceed to Bosaso, Somalia. 118-26 is Somali-basin piracy and is segregated from the Hormuz count. UNRESOLVED AND REPORTED, NOT SMOOTHED: 115-26 (in 086) and 116-26 (in 087) are logged as two separate fatal attacks — 115-26 an engine-room strike 0.5NM off Oman, 116-26 a rocket to the starboard side dated 15 August. Throughput — the Axios convoy claim now has a tracker sitting against it

Axios (19 Aug, two unnamed US officials): a nightly US-escorted corridor along the southern Omani channel, 15–20 tankers each night, close to 10 mn b/d out of the strait, “roughly half pre-war”, run by a task force out of Fort Bragg. “Roughly half” implies a ~20 mn b/d baseline; this document uses ~15 mb/d, on which 10 would be about two thirds. The denominators do not agree and are not reconciled. It was picked up by seven outlets on 20 August and every one traces to Axios; there is no independent Tier 1 verification, no DoD confirmation and no denial. The tension to report — and not to reconcile — is that Windward logged 16 total strait contacts in both directions across all cargo types on 19 August, which is not obviously compatible with 15–20 tankers a night through one corridor unless nearly all of the convoy traffic is undetected. Against both: Kpler puts crude clearance across the 60-day MoU window at 6.1 mb/d, about 40% of the ~15 mb/d Hormuz averaged in 2025, and warns that its own most recent week revises up by a factor of 1.5 to 2.0 — which is now a sourceable basis for this monitor’s rule against computing a day-on-day off a same-day Kpler print. Energy Secretary Wright’s ~15 mn b/d has no update.

CENTCOM combat activity — 23 days, and the one thing it did announce

The public-releases index was read directly. The most recent release describing a strike inside Iran is still 29 July — now a 23-day gap — and the most recent release of any kind is 15 August, on the commander’s regional trip. There is no release dated 20 or 21 August. CENTCOM did nonetheless announce on 20 August that the USS George Washington has ARRIVED IN THEATRE to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after 250-plus days — but the strike group is still transiting the Arabian Sea toward the Gulf of Oman, so the relief is UNDER WAY and not complete; the announcement came through press rather than the releases index, and is reported here as Tier 2 attributed to a CENTCOM statement. Nothing at all on USS George H.W. Bush. Note that the NEWS-ARTICLES index is stale to February 2026 and is not a usable channel — the PUBLIC-RELEASES index is the primary source and must be the one queried.

Red Sea and the wider periphery

Bab el-Mandeb transits ROSE: 71 vessels over the 18–19 August 48 hours, against 59 over 16–17 August — about 35/day against a ~61/day 2023 baseline. Al-Mokha remains completely closed. The one confirmed Red Sea incident in 087, 117-26, destroyed an unmanned, cargo-less hull. The Houthi claim to have struck Aramco’s Jazan refinery on 18 August is now in its fourth day with no Saudi or Aramco comment and no Tier 1 corroboration — carried as a CLAIM only, unlike the confirmed 9 August strike. SIX vessels are now under pirate control — HONOUR 25, SWARD, EUREKA, ASANA, LUTUF and, from 20 August, SEAMULL — and every one of them is Somali-basin piracy, kept strictly segregated from the Hormuz count. NO kinetic event anywhere in the Hormuz theatre is dated 20 or 21 August, and a Tier 2 aggregator puts at 21 the run of nights with no US or Israeli strike inside Iran and no acknowledged coalition air operation anywhere in theatre. That count excludes vessel attacks and is a different measure from the UKMTO incident count, which rose by three in the same window. A circulating attribution of an ADNOC-vessel attack to Friday 21 August is REJECTED: the source page is dated 14 August, which was also a Friday.

The economic-war track — declared, and not yet instrumented

Trump, Truth Social, late 19 August New York time and therefore after the last edition’s Singapore cut: an “ECONOMIC D-DAY”, warning that any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities provide Iran a lifeline will face “tremendous economic consequences”, naming oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies. We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history… we are going to collapse this regime”, and on third countries “you’re either with us or against us”; he declined to say whether China would be targeted, noting the Chinese take about half their energy from inside the Gulf. bondYield.title: (i) Treasury stress — held at 5 (max); the legs rotated apart again and Threshold B re-armed
bondYield.text: The 30-year closed 5.2476%, up 5.65 bp — the largest one-day rise in the tenor since 31 July, and a give-back of 62% of Wednesday’s fall in a single session. MOVE rose 1.92 to 73.18, still below 75 but only 0.20 below the pre-war anchor. The downgrade needs the 30-year below 5.00% with MOVE below 75, sustained. The volatility leg is satisfied for a third consecutive close, the equal-longest run of the current regime. The 30-year leg fails by 24.76 bp — WIDENED straight back out from 19.11. Last edition reported both legs converging for the first time since 13 August; that conclusion is withdrawn, and the standing observation stands: these legs rotate, they do not converge. The forward-looking point has now been demonstrated five separate times: the MOVE leg was satisfied on the 5 and 7 August closes and lost on the next session each time, and Threshold B has re-armed after a single session out on 10 August, on 14 August, and now again. The correct posture toward any single long-end session in this war is that it does not survive contact with the next one. A sustained 30-year below 5.00% with MOVE below 75 takes the channel to 4 and the score to 26. On these levels that requires another 24.76 bp, 5.65 more than a session ago.

bondYield.title: (ii) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max); the downgrade gap widened back out
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y closed 2.3432%, up 3.26 bp and a fifth consecutive close above the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel 4→5 on 31 July, now clear by 4.32 bp — the widest since 12 August. BE10 closed 2.3525%, the highest since 8 June and 9.56 bp above the 2.2569% pre-war anchor. The documented downgrade is a sustained close at or below the 2.142% anchor, 20.12 bp lower — WIDENED from 16.86. The breakeven series is the one to read this week, and it is why this channel’s 5/5 reads comfortably against the tape even as the documented downgrade gap widens. The tension between the firing trigger and the documented downgrade is not resolved by that; it is 3.26 bp worse. On 13 August this document reported BE10 at 0.21 bp above its pre-war anchor and said a single basis point would put spot inflation compensation below pre-war for the first time in the war. Five sessions later it is 9.56 bp the other way — a 9.35 bp rise on the week, against 3.51 bp on the 30-year nominal. Inflation compensation is rebuilding faster than nominal yields are, which is the opposite composition to Wednesday’s buyback session and is consistent with a diesel crack that has been at a record and a retail diesel price making consecutive war highs. Sustained closes at or below 2.142% take the channel to 4 and the score to 26; the move required has grown by 3.26 bp in one session.

bondYield.title: (iii) Oil price shock — held at 2, and a fourth consecutive narrowing of the upgrade gap
bondYield.text: Brent closed $91.97 on the scored CO2 continuation, up $2.18 and the fifth consecutive up-close, the highest since 24 July; the active contract closed $93.78, the highest since 23 July. WTI closed $86.83. The upgrade trigger is a sustained Brent close above $95 and it is $3.03 away on the scored series and $1.22 on the active close — the narrowest either has been since the July roll, and a fourth consecutive edition of narrowing (9.78, 8.43, 5.55, 5.21, 3.03). The named attributions this week are to policy and to risk perception, not to any physical event this document can date. Note that the first named attribution explains an ABSENCE OF DECLINE rather than the rise: Rystad’s Susan Bell told Reuters that “despite the bearish crude stock data, the broader geopolitical backdrop is preventing a sharper price decline”; SEB’s Bjarne Schieldrop attributes the rise to a US approach that implies little hope of near-term resolution; and the most-cited proximate driver in Thursday’s wraps is Bessent’s restatement of the “toughest sanctions in history” threat. Sustained closes above $95 take the channel to 3 and the score to 28 — and the trigger is about to be tested: it requires sustained closes, not a touch, and with the active contract $1.22 away a single print through $95 will not move this score. ROLL DISCLOSURE, and it has its first live occurrence this edition, on WTI. The scored CL2 continuation and the CLA active contract printed identical to the cent on every session from 3 to 20 August and diverge by $1.93 on the 21 August row. The apparent –$2.46 day-on-day move in WTI is therefore a roll artifact and is not reported as a price move; on the active contract the fall is 53 cents. Separately, the CLA column has been RESTATED across the whole 3–20 August window: the 19 August active close this monitor published as $85.83 now reads $84.39, and the active Brent–WTI spread is consequently not comparable with the figures published before 21 August. On Brent the position is unchanged from last edition and must be restated because it governs every distance quoted above: the scored CO2 continuation closed $100.69 on 23 July and $96.78 on 24 July, two consecutive closes above the $95 trigger, while the ACTIVE contract closed $94.26 and $91.68 on the same two days, below it. The correct formulation remains that the last two closes above $95 sit on the far side of a July roll on which the active contract never cleared the trigger, and that every distance in this edition is measured on the current post-roll basis. The CO2/COA basis — the continuation minus the active contract, which is a different quantity from the reconciliation gaps and happens to share a figure with them — has narrowed from $1.92 below on the 20 Aug intraday to $1.81 below on the 20 Aug close, so the two measures are converging rather than diverging, which matters because at $1.22 the active gap is now the binding one on any reading. The material one for this channel is 116-26: a bulk carrier attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on 15 August, a rocket to the starboard side under the gangway, one confirmed crew fatality, vessel not under command. All nine threat levels are unchanged and Hormuz remains SEVERE. The annex now extends to 19 August and shows Hormuz cargo transits of 0, 1 and 0 across 17–19 August with tankers at 3, 3 and 3 — a combined 3, 4 and 3 a day against a ~138/day all-transits baseline. The channel cannot rise: it is at the cap, and further deterioration in the physical situation cannot raise this score, so a flat number is an artifact of the scale rather than a statement about stability. The documented downgrade — a verified reopening with traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions — is not remotely in view.

bondYield.title: (vi) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max), against a kinetic record that went empty while the economic front escalated
bondYield.text: Neither event channel can rise, and this edition is the cleanest illustration of what that costs the reader, because the two capped channels moved in opposite directions and the total could register neither. On the kinetic side the record is emptier than at any point in weeks: no kinetic event anywhere in the Hormuz theatre dated 20 or 21 August, a 23-day CENTCOM combat silence inside Iran, a carrier relief under way without reported incident, and UKMTO’s own assessment that attack frequency “has remained consistent” in what it calls an “established post-MoU status quo”. On the economic side Washington escalated to a declared objective: Trump’s “Economic D-Day” and a Treasury Secretary saying on CNBC “we are going to collapse this regime”, with third countries told “you’re either with us or against us” and China explicitly not ruled out. An embargo, a sanctions threat and a stated intent to collapse a government are not kinetic events and are not scored as ones; they are scored as what they remove from the negotiating space, which is why they show up in the scenario map rather than in the total. The documented downgrade — a mediated stand-down with talks resuming — is further away than it has been, since the counterparty’s stated aim is now the other side’s collapse.

analysis.stage4Note: Stage 4 is a credit and auction event, tested on confirmed closes and on primary auction results only. stage4.title: Threshold A · a failed-auction test — NOT ARMED, and the test is now UNTESTABLE AS WRITTEN
stage4.text: A is a failed-auction test: an auction clearing with a tail above its when-issued level. Treasury’s own primary results for the 19 August 20-year were retrieved this edition via the Fiscal Data auctions API (release R_20260819_2, CUSIP 912810UX4) — the TreasuryDirect PDF endpoints return empty to a fetcher, and the API is the standing route from now on. Bid-to-cover of 2.53 is CONFIRMED exactly; the high yield is 5.2040%. The 62.9% indirect share this monitor carried as single-sourced is CORRECT — on the competitive-accepted denominator, where it is 62.93%. On total award ex-SOMA it is 62.17%. It was a denominator artifact, not an error, and the rule that every percentage must name its denominator applies to auction allotments too. THE 0.5 bp TAIL CANNOT BE CONFIRMED FROM ANY TREASURY SOURCE, because Treasury does not publish a when-issued level at all. Last edition left A conditional on primary confirmation of that tail; the honest answer is that no such confirmation can ever exist, so the condition is untestable as written and must be replaced rather than left pending. That is recorded as an open item and not disposed of here. The standing instruction to read the bid composition is where the story is: primary dealers took just 12.34% of the 20-year award, and on the $8bn 30-year TIPS reopening the next day they took 2.09% — tendering $11.9bn and being awarded $167m — against indirects at 83.85% and a bid-to-cover of 2.82. That TIPS cleared a real yield of 2.9730%, described by Tipswatch (Tier 2) as the highest for the tenor since October 2001. Two consecutive long-end auctions cleared with minimal dealer participation — indirects at 62.93% and 83.85%, dealers at 12.34% and 2.09% — and neither allotment split appeared in any wire report this desk could retrieve; the figures here come from Treasury’s own release data. Context: the 30-year closed 3.16 bp ABOVE the 13 August stop and 19.76 bp above the 13 May stop.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — RE-ARMED, after exactly one session out
stage4.text: RE-ARMED on the 20 August close, after exactly one session out. The 30-year clears by 4.76 bp and the 10-year by 5.41 bp. This is the FIFTH arming and the ninth state since 29 July — in 29 Jul–3 Aug, out 4–5 Aug, in 6 Aug, out 7 Aug, in 10–12 Aug, out 13 Aug, in 14–18 Aug, out 19 Aug, in 20 Aug. Five armings, four lapses. Count armings, not cycles. The lapse that just ended lasted a single session and was decided by 0.89 and 0.34 bp — the narrowest margins of the war — which is exactly why the hysteresis discipline exists. This is the THIRD time B has re-armed within one session, after 10 and 14 August; the 6 August re-arming followed a TWO-session lapse and is not one of them. The inference that has held since 13 August still holds and gets stronger with every cycle: 4.65% and 5.20% are the middle of the distribution, not its edge, and all eight state changes have been decided by under 6 bp on one leg.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130 — not armed, and the pairing narrowed on one side
stage4.text: 73.18 on the 20 August close, 56.82 points below, having risen 1.92. The war high is 115.02 (26 March) and the series low 65.39 (18 June), so this is NOT the furthest from C the war has been. The pairing has narrowed on one side and widened on the other: rate volatility is now only 0.20 below its pre-war anchor, against 2.12 below a session ago, while the 30-year sits 63.70 bp above its own, against 58.05. This is a market that has priced the movement out of rates while the level of the long bond has gone further from normal.

analysis.crossAsset: Four US releases landed on the morning of 20 August and every one of them came in at or above consensus. The Philadelphia Fed’s August manufacturing index printed +47.4, which the Bank reports as a five-year high, from 41.4 in July — a very large upside surprise on any of the consensus figures in circulation, which ranged from 6.3 to 25.0, and the spread of those consensus figures is itself a caveat on how big the “surprise” was. Initial jobless claims fell 6,000 to 206,000. Existing home sales came in at 4.05M SAAR against a 3.94M consensus, a second consecutive monthly decline but a beat, with the median price at $434,100 and a 37th straight month of annual gains. The Conference Board’s leading index rose 0.2% and its six-month growth rate turned positive at +0.2% from –1.3%. The long end sold off through all of it, which is the ordinary and expected response and is precisely why it matters here: it means Wednesday’s 9 bp rally was not a repricing of risk but a repricing of supply, and one strong data day was enough to take most of it back. A Fed official said the same thing in different words, speaking only for himself. St. Louis’s Alberto Musalem told CNBC on 20 August that the bond selloff reflects “a competition for capital… from government financing… plus the AI build-out” and not a Fed credibility problem; that policy is still “accommodative” with the real funds rate below neutral; and that underlying inflation is running 2.5–3% against a 2% target. He declined to prejudge September. September pricing sits at roughly a 68% hold on a 20 August reading — but that figure comes through a secondary aggregator citing CME FedWatch, not from CME directly, and no clean datestamped CME print could be sourced for a second consecutive edition. Jackson Hole runs 27–29 August on “Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy”, with Chair Warsh’s first keynote on Friday 28 August — nineteen days before the 16 September FOMC; the Kansas City Fed’s own programme still could not be retrieved and the agenda remains Tier 2. GDPNow is unchanged at 4.0% for Q3, dated 18 August, with the next revision on 26 August. On the economic-war track, the rhetoric ran well ahead of the instrument. Trump announced an “ECONOMIC D-DAY” late on 19 August New York time — after the last edition’s Singapore cut — warning that any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities provide Iran a lifeline will face “tremendous economic consequences”, naming oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies. Bessent followed on CNBC on 20 August: “It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history… we are going to collapse this regime”, and on third countries “you’re either with us or against us”. He declined to say whether China would be targeted, noting that the Chinese take about half their energy from inside the Gulf. What actually issued on 20 August is not that package. OFAC’s action of that date designates ten individuals in a Hizballah cash-smuggling network, three of them tagged as linked to the IRGC-Qods Force, and amends Hizballah’s own SDN entry to carry an IRGC-QF designation. The designees are mostly Turkey-based and two carry UAE addresses. There is no Iranian oil, shipping, refinery, bank, ship-registry or vessel designation, no Iran-related executive order and no new general licence; the only vessels added that day are Ecuadorian fishing boats under the counter-narcotics programme. On the third day after “Economic D-Day”, on this document’s inclusive count, the Hormuz-facing sanctions remain undelivered. China’s foreign ministry said on 20 August that “imposing sanctions and pressuring do not help to solve the issue”. On the regional track, Majlis Speaker Ghalibaf’s three-day visit to Iraq, which opened in Baghdad on 19 August and takes in Karbala and Najaf, concludes on Friday 21 August; no readout from the Karbala or Najaf legs has been published. A single-sourced report that he discussed an Iranian plan to conceal militia weapons is confirmed by neither government and is NOT used. Iran’s answer came from Araghchi the same morning: the “so-called Economic D-Day” is “a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt and surging interest costs”. Whatever its motive, it names the transmission channel this document tracks, and it is the government the mechanism is aimed at that named it; the characterisation of the debt level as “unprecedented” is Araghchi’s and is not tested here. Elsewhere on the energy and freight record, most of the standing figures did not refresh and are labelled rather than rolled forward. No EIA, IEA, OPEC or OPEC+ release dated 20 or 21 August; the next OPEC+ meeting is 6 September and effective OPEC spare capacity of 0.07 mb/d, a 3Q26 deficit of 1.8 mb/d and 8.3 mb/d shut in all survive unrevised. The Baltic week-34 tanker averages could not be retrieved and are reported as not obtained, NOT as unchanged; week 33 was VLCC $234,821/day, Suezmax $269,824/day and Aframax $77,182/day. Lloyd’s List assessed TD3C MEG–China above $520,000/day on 19 August — a single route, never comparable with the global VLCC average, and Lloyd’s List itself has described Middle East VLCC index rates in this crisis as thinly underpinned. War-risk cover still has nothing newer than Marsh’s 7.5–10% of hull of 22 July; a “3–8% of vessel value” range circulating as industry estimate has no named broker and is not used, and straits.live’s “40x normal” is its own model, not a quote. The covert relay is unchanged rather than deepened: Windward reported on 19 August that two Hong Kong-flagged, Chinese-managed tankers aborted Hormuz transits within 24 hours, one broadcasting “CHINESE CREW OWNER” in its AIS destination field, and that China’s two largest state operators are keeping fleets out of both chokepoints on Beijing’s guidance; Kharg saw its first terminal activity in 23 days, a dark vessel at the sulphur and LPG berth — “a marginal signal… not yet a clear reversal”. Iranian crude loadings remain 156 kb/d through 17 August against 893 kb/d in July, and crude on water in the Mideast Gulf and Gulf of Oman 110 mn bbl on 18 August; neither has a 20 or 21 August update. DP World is spending about $100m a month keeping Jebel Ali ready to reopen against container throughput at roughly 10% of pre-crisis levels, and ADNOC L&S has disclosed $1.3bn of VLCC and VLGC purchases — balance-sheet positioning for a long closure.

methodology.scale: Shock-score scale. Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger, never on an intraday print. Maritime denial and escalation risk are event-based and move on events, not announcements: a declared posture, a stated objective, an agreed-but-unissued declaration or a trailed sanctions package is not an event. Hysteresis is asymmetric by design: a channel is upgraded on a sustained break of its trigger and downgraded only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold. This edition is the strongest vindication of that property the document has produced: the previous session’s 9 bp long-end rally, its lapsed Stage-4 threshold and its three-month dollar low were all undone or materially given back within one close — 62% of the rally, the lapse entirely, the dollar low as a trend — and no score moved on any of them, because none met a documented rule. The cost is also visible: the US-inflation channel fired on a 2.30% break in the 5-year-five-year forward and its documented downgrade sits at the 2.142% pre-war anchor, 20.12 bp below Thursday’s close. The gap is reported rather than closed, and the rule is not moved to match the tape.
methodology.scaleCap: The saturated scale. Five of the six channels are at 5; only oil, at 2, is not — three points below the cap, not one. Further deterioration in the strait or in the political situation cannot raise the total, so a flat score is an artifact of the scale rather than a statement about stability, and the same failure runs in reverse when everything improves, as it did on 14 August. This edition is a fourth variant, and the sharpest yet: the two capped channels moved in OPPOSITE directions. Maritime denial worsened — UKMTO Update 087 added three confirmed incidents and took the cumulative count from 91 to 94, including a rocket attack with a crew fatality in the strait itself. Escalation, on the kinetic measure, went empty — no event anywhere in the theatre dated 20 or 21 August, a 23-day CENTCOM combat silence, and the primary source itself describing an “established post-MoU status quo”. Meanwhile the United States declared an economic war whose stated aim, as put by a cabinet officer on television, is the collapse of the Iranian government. The total registered none of it. Readers should attend to the composition and to the distance-to-trigger figures, reported in basis points and dollars precisely so that movement inside a frozen total remains visible.

2026-08-26.headline: Score HOLDS at 27/30 for a twelfth consecutive edition. No channel moved. The week’s event is that the diplomatic track produced its first written instrument since the Islamabad Memorandum while the physical strait recorded its thinnest traffic since early May — and the oil price traded the paper, not the water. On 25 August Iran and Oman ISSUED a joint statement in Tehran naming a temporary joint maritime corridor, a joint mine-clearance project and a track to a permanent corridor. It is not a reopening, and Tehran said so the same day: Araghchi conditions reopening on Washington honouring a memorandum that LAPSED on 17 August, and Busaidi cites that dead document’s Article 5 as the corridor’s legal basis. That circularity is why the escalation channel does not move — an announcement is not an event, and US–Iran talks have not resumed and none are scheduled. The only channel with headroom went the wrong way: Brent closed $87.27 after two consecutive down-closes from $92.67 and printed $85.31 intraday, so the edition-over-edition upgrade gap widened from $3.03 to $7.73 on the scored CO2 series and from $1.22 to $6.42 on the active — the first widening after four narrowings, on a headline rather than a barrel. The dissonance this edition is built on is that in the same 48 hours UKMTO’s annex recorded one cargo vessel and zero tankers through the strait on 24 August, Kpler counted two commodity vessels — its thinnest day since early May against a 10-day average of 14 — and Windward recorded four transits, ALL INBOUND, with no vessel transiting outbound at all. A market pricing a reopening into a waterway that has just stopped letting ships out has not verified anything. Stage-4 Threshold B LAPSED on the 25 August close, on BOTH legs at once, short of 5.20% and 4.65% by 3.49 and 2.12 bp; the fifth arming lasted three closes, making this the sixth lapse, the eleventh state and the tenth change since 29 July. And the edition’s most consequential finding is that the standing observation that the two Treasury downgrade legs rotate rather than converge, which has held since 6 August, stopped being true: on 25 August they converged, with MOVE falling to 71.92 for a sixth consecutive close below 75 while the 30-year gap narrowed to 16.51 bp, the narrowest since 28 July. It still fails and hysteresis requires sustained, so the channel holds at 5 — but this is now the live downgrade candidate of the document. Washington escalated on 24 August with roughly 60 designations and five NEW E.O. 13902 sector determinations, and withheld the heaviest instrument: no Chinese refinery, port or bank. Within 24 hours Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Gargash all pushed the other way; the coalition is not following the rhetoric. Finally, diesel decoupled from gasoline: AAA diesel reached $5.6199, a new war high, 19.60 cents from its record, while all-grades gasoline — the series the political channel is actually scored on — did not move at all and AAA regular FELL. The routing shock is arriving in freight fuel, not at the pump.

analysis.intro: The score holds at 27/30 for a twelfth consecutive edition and no channel moved, but the composition this week is a genuine dissonance rather than a saturation artifact. The diplomatic record improved materially — a written framework naming a corridor and a demining project, a live Pakistani channel, three Gulf capitals pushing publicly toward de-escalation, twenty-six nights with no strike inside Iran and a 28-day CENTCOM combat silence. The physical record deteriorated at the same time: one cargo vessel and no tankers on the UKMTO annex for 24 August, Kpler’s thinnest day since early May, and Windward recording no outbound transit at all. The oil price traded the first of those and ignored the second. Read the composition, not the total, and note that the only channel with headroom moved AWAY from its upgrade in the same week the market priced a reopening.

bondYield.title: (i) Treasury stress — held at 5 (max), and for the first time in the war the two downgrade legs CONVERGED
bondYield.text: The downgrade needs a 30-year close below 5.00% together with MOVE below 75, sustained. The standing observation since 6 August has been that these legs rotate rather than approach: one is satisfied while the other widens. THAT STOPPED BEING TRUE ON 25 AUGUST. The 30-year closed 5.1651%, down 5.94 bp and its lowest close since the 5.0886% of 28 July, taking the yield leg’s shortfall to 16.51 bp — the narrowest since 28 July — on a run of 27.09 → 22.45 → 16.51 across the three sessions. MOVE closed 71.92, its sixth consecutive close below 75. BE EXACT ABOUT 24 AUGUST: MOVE ROSE that day, 73.40 to 73.98, while the yield gap narrowed, so 24 August is still rotation. It is 25 August on which both legs moved toward the downgrade in the same session. On the volatility leg, bound the superlative properly: six consecutive closes below 75 is NOT a war record — the war has seen runs of 21 sessions from 10 June, 17 from 9 April, 8 from 26 May and 7 from 6 May — but it is the longest run since 10 June–10 July and double the best the regime that began on 29 July had produced (three closes, 12–14 August). The standing warning that a single sub-threshold close is a session and not a regime has been the right call four times; on the sixth consecutive close it stops applying, and this document says so. The yield leg still fails, and that is what holds the score: the rule requires a close below 5.00% SUSTAINED, and the 26 August intraday has already widened the gap back to 17.34 bp. The honest statement is that this is the live downgrade candidate of the document and that a 16.51 bp gap sits comfortably inside a single session’s range in either direction. A sustained 30-year below 5.00% with MOVE below 75 takes the channel to 4 and the score to 26.

bondYield.title: (ii) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and the firing trigger broke for a second time
bondYield.text: Lead with the adverse fact. The 5-year five-year forward closed 2.2991% on 25 August, BELOW the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel from 4 to 5 on 31 July. It is the second such close in the current regime, after 2.2900% on 13 August, and it has NOT been confirmed by a second close — the 26 August intraday reads 2.3051%, back above the line, but a snapshot settles nothing, and 13 August was likewise retraced on the 14 August close. The documented downgrade is a sustained close at or below the 2.142% pre-war anchor, still 15.71 bp lower, so the score holds at 5 — and the rule is NOT being moved to meet the trigger. That gap between the firing level and the downgrade level is uncomfortable and it is published rather than closed; converting it into a symmetric trigger would destroy the property that has stopped five bad calls since late July. The 15.71 bp is nonetheless the narrowest reading since the 14.80 of 13 August, having been 20.12 bp on 20 August. The corroborating series agrees and says it more starkly: ten-year breakeven compensation closed 2.3135%, just 5.66 bp above its 2.2569% pre-war anchor, having been 9.56 bp above it on 20 August when it reached its highest since 8 June. The two series have retraced by different amounts — BE10 by more than a third of its distance from pre-war, 5y5y by about a fifth — in three sessions, in a week in which diesel set a war high. That is a market pricing the shock as a relative-price event rather than a price-level regime: the reading this channel has resisted since it fired to 5 on 31 July, and it is now the closest it has come to being right. Sustained closes at or below 2.142% take the channel to 4 and the score to 26.

bondYield.title: (iii) Oil price shock — held at 2, and the upgrade gap WIDENED for the first time in six readings
bondYield.text: Brent closed $87.27 on the scored CO2 continuation after TWO consecutive down-closes from $92.67 — 21 August was an up-close, so there is no third — and printed $85.31 intraday on 26 August, its lowest since the 13 August close of $85.22. The sequence of edition-over-edition distances to the $95 upgrade now reads 9.78, 8.43, 5.55, 5.21, 3.03, 7.73: SIX readings, four narrowings, then one widening. On the active contract it runs $1.22 to $6.42. On the intervening closes this edition publishes in full, the gap narrowed further to $2.33 on 21 August before widening to $4.46 on 24 August and $7.73 on 25 August — so the true low was $2.33 and the widening began on 24 August, not 25. THE CAUSE IS A HEADLINE, NOT A BARREL. The daily wraps attribute the fall to the Iran–Oman corridor talks being priced as de-escalation. Set that against the physical data in the same window — the thinnest transit day since early May, no outbound traffic at all, and Kpler’s own measure of China’s Iranian crude imports at 534 kb/d month-to-date against ~823 in July and a 1.4 mb/d 2025 average — and the market is trading an announcement that Araghchi, its Iranian principal, said the same day does not open the strait. THE ROLL DISCLOSURE STANDS AND THE BASIS CHECK CLEARS: the CO2/COA basis has compressed smoothly from 1.81 to 1.02 across the window with no sign change and no step, so there is no Brent roll in this data; the WTI roll of 21 August is behind us and CL2/CLA now move together. The July roll artifact remains an OPEN methodological item — the scored continuation closed above $95 on 23 and 24 July, days on which the active contract closed $94.26 and $91.68 and never cleared the trigger — so never write that Brent has not closed above $95 since the channel was cut to 2 on 3 July. It has, twice. The downgrade needs a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48; the price leg is $14.79 away and moved further away this week even as the mediation leg moved closer. Both legs of the oil downgrade have now decoupled from each other, which is the first time this document has had to say that. Sustained closes above $95 take the channel to 3 and the score to 28.

bondYield.title: (iv) Political stress — held at 5 (max), and the interesting movement is in a series this channel does not score
bondYield.text: The scored AUTMUSAG all-grades series reads $4.82, its fourth consecutive identical print, 22 cents above the named $4.60 downgrade condition and seven cents above the $4.75 trigger that fired the upgrade. Under the field-level rule the 24 August value is identical to four decimal places to 21 August and is therefore reported UNRESOLVED with no day-on-day asserted. The direct reads say the pump is flat to slightly lower — AAA regular moved $4.1044 (20 Aug) to $4.0991 (24 Aug) to $4.0969 (25 Aug), BELOW where it stood at the last edition and below its month-ago level, while the EIA weekly regular survey printed $4.085 for the 24 August week, up 3.6 cents. Note what that does and does not establish: a different series cannot certify this one, so AUTMUSAG stays UNRESOLVED; what the direct read establishes is that the national pump is flat. DIESEL IS WHERE THE SHOCK ACTUALLY IS, AND IT HAS DECOUPLED. AAA diesel reached $5.6199 on 25 August, a new war high, 19.60 cents from the all-time record of $5.8159, up 15.22 cents in seven days and 34.21 in a month; the EIA weekly on-highway series printed $5.652, up 19.8 cents after 19.7 the week before — two consecutive weeks of nearly twenty cents — with California at $7.040 and the Gulf Coast up 24.4 cents. Two such weekly rises in the freight fuel while the consumer fuel drifts lower is the signature of a routing and refining dislocation rather than a crude-price pass-through, and it is invisible to the series this channel is scored on. The score is right; the scored series is telling you less than the one beside it. The named condition, met three times running, takes the channel to 4 and the score to 26.

bondYield.title: (v) Maritime denial — held at 5 (max), and the traffic leg of the downgrade moved AWAY this week
bondYield.text: The downgrade needs a verified reopening plus traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. Neither leg is close, and the traffic leg moved away. On 24 August the UKMTO annex recorded one cargo vessel and no tankers; Kpler counted two commodity ships, its thinnest day since early May against its own 10-day average of 14; Windward recorded four transits and NOT ONE OUTBOUND, which it reads as active enforcement against southbound traffic at the blockade line; TankerMap counted one tanker. Name the denominator every time, and note that one has now changed under us: UKMTO and Windward both use roughly 138–140 vessels a day, Kpler uses a ~15 mb/d volume basis, and IMF PortWatch’s own JSON now returns a pre-crisis median of 85/day against the 73/day its front page has been publishing — the same series, two different numbers — so this document will not quote a PortWatch percentage without saying which divisor produced it. Update 089 takes the cumulative incident count from 94 to 96 and the blockade tally to 71 redirected. The Gulf of Oman threat-level cut is the first reduction this monitor has recorded and it is NOT evidence of de-escalation: UKMTO’s own stated reasoning is that the strikes have been reclassified into the Hormuz bucket, and the Hormuz level is unchanged at SEVERE. A vessel disabled by a projectile in Omani waters on 24 August, roughly twenty-four hours before the Strait was declared mine-free, is the more informative datum. The channel cannot rise: it is at the cap, so a flat number is an artifact of the scale rather than a statement about stability.

bondYield.title: (vi) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max), and this is the closest the war has come to a downgrade case
bondYield.text: The case FOR moving is real and should be stated at full strength. Iran and Oman issued a joint statement naming a temporary corridor and joint demining; Pakistan’s army chief carried a reopening agenda into Tehran on 24 August; Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE all pushed publicly toward de-escalation within 24 hours of Washington escalating; there has been no US or Israeli strike inside Iran and no Iranian launch across the whole window; and CENTCOM’s combat silence has reached 28 days. Hegseth on 24 August: “Economic pressure is what we know hurts them the most.” IT IS HELD ANYWAY, AND THE REASON IS THAT AN ANNOUNCEMENT IS NOT AN EVENT. On 2 August this monitor declined an escalation downgrade on a cancelled strike package and announced talks, and was right within days. The identical structure is present now: talks have not convened, none are scheduled, and Araghchi, the framework’s Iranian principal, said the same day that it does not open the strait. And the counter-evidence inside the window is not thin. Two vessels were struck on 24 August — one DISABLED in Omani waters, and one off Yanbu in the Red Sea under a Houthi claim, which is NOT a Hormuz event and is named as such so the pair is not read as two Hormuz attacks. A parliamentary commission approved a Hormuz transit-fee article (Tier 3 sourcing, and not enacted legislation), and Iran blacklisted 46 ships per gCaptain or 45 tankers per Reuters — two counts on different units, reported and not reconciled. SNSC Secretary Rezaei raised nuclear-weapons acquisition on state television on 23 August and on 24 August named Saudi and Emirati bypass pipelines as within the target set — Tier 2 reporting of Tier 3 source material, single-stream, with no Tier 1 wire pickup located, and flagged as such rather than used to move a probability. The mediated-pause scenario moves in section 5; the channel does not. The documented downgrade — a mediated stand-down with talks resuming — has its stand-down leg closer than at any point in the war and its talks leg entirely unmoved.

stage4.title: Threshold A · a failed-auction test — NOT ARMED, and UNTESTABLE AS WRITTEN rather than merely unverified
stage4.text: A is a failed-auction test — an auction clearing with a tail above its when-issued level — and Treasury publishes no when-issued level at all, so no primary source can ever confirm a tail. The clearing statistics are reachable every time and are the substitute. The 25 August 2-year (CUSIP 91282CRH6, $69bn) cleared at a high yield of 4.2040% with bid-to-cover 2.60 computed ex-SOMA on Treasury’s own convention, and 85.68% allotted at the high. NAME THE DENOMINATOR: primary dealers took 10.90% on competitive-accepted and 10.76% on total-award-ex-SOMA; indirects 66.01% and 65.16%; directs 23.09% and 22.79%. Note that computing bid-to-cover on raw totals gives 2.42 rather than 2.60 and is a common error. THE COMPOSITION IS THE SIGNAL, AND IT IS NOW A RUN: three consecutive coupon auctions have cleared with a primary-dealer backstop in single or low double digits — 12.34% on the 20-year (19 Aug), 2.09% on the $8bn 30-year TIPS (20 Aug), and 10.90% here. Paper is clearing, and it is clearing away from dealers. The $70bn 5-year and the $28bn 2-year FRN were auctioned on 26 August after the Singapore cut and their results are NOT OBTAINED; the $44bn 7-year falls on 27 August. One loose end: the 2-year carries a special announcement, SPL_20260820_1.pdf, which returned empty to a fetcher and is NOT OBTAINED. stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — LAPSED, and both legs failed in the same session
stage4.text: On the 25 August close the 30-year closed 5.1651%, short by 3.49 bp, and the 10-year 4.6288%, short by 2.12 bp. The fifth arming ran three closes — 20, 21 and 24 August — which is consistent with the pattern that EIGHT of the previous NINE states lasted three closes or fewer and four lasted exactly one. THIS IS THE SIXTH LAPSE, THE ELEVENTH STATE AND THE TENTH CHANGE SINCE 29 JULY. The full sequence: in 29 Jul–3 Aug, out 4–5 Aug, in 6 Aug, out 7 Aug, in 10–12 Aug, out 13 Aug, in 14–18 Aug, out 19 Aug, in 20–24 Aug, out 25 Aug. Five armings, six lapses; count armings, not cycles. It remains lapsed on the 26 August intraday, where the 30-year is 2.66 bp short and the 10-year 1.33 bp short — both margins inside a single session’s range, so a re-arm on the 26 August close would be the FOURTH one-session round trip, after 10, 14 and 20 August. The inference that has held since 13 August still holds and gets stronger with every cycle: 4.65% and 5.20% are the middle of the distribution, not its edge.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130 — not armed, and the pairing is more durable than at any point since early July
stage4.text: 71.92 on the 25 August close, 58.08 points below the trigger. Bound the superlative properly: this is NOT the furthest MOVE has been from C in the war — the series low is 65.39 on 18 June — but it is the lowest close since the 71.26 of 19 August, and the war high of 115.02 (26 March) is more than 43 points away. The number that matters remains the pairing: MOVE sits 1.46 points BELOW its pre-war anchor while the 30-year sits 55.45 bp ABOVE its own. A fully normalised expectation of movement around a yield that has not normalised at all — and, six sessions into the volatility regime, that pairing is more durable than at any point since early July.

analysis.crossAsset: The 25 August US session was a risk-on, duration-friendly one driven by soft domestic data, not by the Gulf. Conference Board consumer confidence printed 89.4 against a 90.2 consensus and a 90.2 prior — the weakest since January — with the Present Situation index up 6.8 to 121.2, its first rise in four months, and Expectations down 5.8 to 68.2, below the 80 recession threshold. The survey period was 3–16 August. Its write-in commentary is directly on this monitor’s subject: references to prices in general “and oil and gas specifically — remain elevated”, and comments about war and conflict ROSE in August. The Board publishes no numeric inflation expectation, only that directional phrase, and no number is invented for it here. New home sales for July fell 10.5% month-on-month to 607,000 SAAR and 6.3% year-on-year, with inventory at 488,000, 9.6 months’ supply, and a median price of $393,800, the lowest in over a year. S&P Cotality Case-Shiller’s 20-city index rose 2.1% year-on-year for June, from 1.6%, with the national index at 1.5% and the 10-city at 2.9%; Chicago at 6.9% and New York at 4.8% led while Seattle fell 2.0%. That is a thirteenth consecutive month in which home values fell in REAL terms against the 3.5% inflation the index benchmarks to. The Chicago Fed National Activity Index for July printed –0.08 from +0.06, with the three-month average at –0.04, the swing driven by personal consumption and housing at –0.09 from +0.04. One dating correction: the 206,000 initial claims print for the week to 15 August was released on 20 August, TWO days before this window opens, and is not dated into it; the next release is 27 August. Three releases fall inside the window but land AFTER the Singapore cut and are therefore NOT OBTAINED — durable goods for July, the second estimate of Q2 GDP, and July PCE, all at 08:30 ET on 26 August. For reference the Q2 advance print was +1.5% SAAR with a gross domestic purchases price index of +5.7% against +3.6% in Q1, which is the energy shock’s signature in the national accounts, and June PCE ran –0.1% month-on-month headline and +0.1% core, +3.7% and +3.3% year-on-year. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still reads 4.0%, dated 18 August; the 26 August revision had not posted, and a 4.0% Q3 nowcast against a 1.5% Q2 advance print is a very wide gap that is model-driven rather than consensus. The 26 August EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, due 10:30 ET, is also NOT OBTAINED, so crude stocks, the crude imports line, refinery runs, product stocks and — critically — whether the SPR drew again from 293.4 mn bbl are all unknown. The standing figures from the week to 14 August: commercial crude 428.8 mn bbl, up 4.4 mn; SPR 293.4 mn bbl, DOWN 5.3 mn on the week from 298.7 mn, against 403.4 mn a year ago and roughly 415 mn pre-war, the lowest since 1982/83; crude imports 6.6 mb/d, down 746 kb/d, on a four-week average of 6.5 mb/d, which supersedes the ~6.3 mb/d carried in prior editions; refinery utilisation 97.2%; and distillate stocks 105.6 mn bbl, about 13% below the five-year average. No EIA STEO, IEA OMR or OPEC MOMR falls in this window; all are mid-month publications. On rates and the Fed, a standing framing needs correcting: the live risk is a September HIKE, not a cut. The 28–29 July FOMC held at 3.50–3.75% on a 9–3 vote with all three dissents FOR A HIKE — Hammack, Kashkari and Logan. No probability is stated here, because a direct CME FedWatch print could not be obtained — the tool is a JavaScript embed that returns nothing to a fetcher — and the only figures in circulation are Tier 3 and put a hike near 40%, which is a live risk rather than a market that is priced for one. The better-sourced alternative is J.P. Morgan Wealth Management’s 5 August move to a 25 bp September hike base case, whose chief investment strategist named “a slower-than-expected normalization of supply chains around the Strait of Hormuz” as a reason. No Federal Reserve Board speech falls between 5 and 26 August — a verified silence rather than a search failure, and no causal gloss is offered for it, since the FOMC blackout runs to a meeting rather than to a symposium. Jackson Hole runs 27–29 August on “Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy”, with Chair Warsh’s first keynote at 10:00 ET on Friday 28 August; the full programme is NOT RETRIEVABLE, and because the 2026 theme is payments rather than supply shocks, any signal on the energy shock will come outside the formal programme. On buybacks, the 19 August announcement raising long-end operations from $2bn to at least $4bn each between 9 September and 4 November is confirmed against Treasury release sb0607, but no updated schedule has been published and is NOT OBTAINED; a 24 August report that Bessent could tap the Treasury General Account to fund them is anonymously sourced and attributed to the outlet rather than to Treasury. On sanctions, OFAC acted on 24 August and it is the only Iran action in the window — Recent Actions shows nothing on 22, 23, 25 or 26 August. “Operation Economic Outcast” designated roughly 60 targets across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland, Malaysia, the UK and France, per Treasury releases sb0613 and sb0614. The structurally important element is FIVE NEW E.O. 13902 SECTOR DETERMINATIONS — aviation, digital assets, gold, shipping and technology — which broaden secondary-sanctions EXPOSURE rather than hitting a marquee target. General licences F and G were suspended and AA and BB issued; five vessels were designated with IMOs, all on flag-of-convenience registries; and the Chinese entities hit are procurement and shadow-banking fronts, not refiners. A Hormuz-specific instrument exists but is GUIDANCE rather than enforcement: an updated OFAC alert on “Sanctions Risks of Iranian Demands for Strait of Hormuz Passage”, the direct counterpart to Iran’s transit-fee law. THE OMISSION IS THE ANALYSIS: no Chinese teapot refinery, no Chinese port, no Chinese bank, no new Iranian bank, no new executive order — the Federal Register confirms — and no ship-registry operator. Asked why he was threatening rather than penalising, Bessent said: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” He set a countdown instead and signalled a financial-institution designation “before end of week”, which lands on top of Warsh’s Friday keynote and is a live catalyst for 27–28 August. China’s foreign ministry opposed the measures on 25 August; no Chinese counter-sanction, and no EU, UK or UN action, could be found. On the physical and freight record, Windward reported on 24–25 August that the Kharg Island dark-tanker waiting area holds 20 dark tankers carrying an assessed 21–23 mn bbl combined, and that a Nicaragua-flagged tanker broadcasting the name SYRON is assessed loading at Kharg’s eastern terminal, its IMO matching SARAK, an OFAC-sanctioned Iranian tanker dark since 20 July. Kpler via Reuters on 21 August put Iranian crude stored aboard tankers OUTSIDE the US blockade zone at roughly 80 mn bbl, from about 105 mn before the blockade was reinstated on 13 July — and that is a DIFFERENT series from the 110 mn bbl of 18 August, which was crude on water INSIDE the Mideast Gulf and Gulf of Oman, so 110 → 80 is not printed as a decline. China’s Iranian crude imports ran 534 kb/d month-to-date in August against roughly 823 kb/d in July and a 1.4 mb/d 2025 average. An updated Iranian loading rate in kb/d for 18–26 August is NOT OBTAINED — the 156 kb/d through 17 August has no successor, and Kpler’s weekly MoU series concluded on 19 August. AMARA, IMO 9333280, Liberia-flagged, has been held stationary near Qeshm Island since 20 August, consistent with an ongoing seizure; no party has confirmed it, and if it is one it is the first Iranian seizure since 22 June. On freight there is a methodology break to disclose: the week-33 aggregate TCE figures this monitor has been carrying — VLCC $234,821/day, Suezmax $269,824, Aframax $77,182 — come from an AGGREGATE SUMMARY series that the week-34 Baltic report does not contain, so a like-for-like week-34 aggregate is NOT OBTAINED and route-level figures are not a continuation of that series. Baltic week 34, dated 21 August, at route level: VLCC TD3C MEG–China at WS570, up 88 points, on a round-trip TCE of about $585,000/day; TD34 Gulf of Oman–China about $197,800/day; Suezmax TD20 above $165,000/day; Aframax TD7 about $93,200/day. Week 35 is due 28 August. Lloyd’s List assessed TD3C above $520,000/day on 19 August, which is a different assessment on a different basis and is not a time series with Baltic’s. On war risk there is an explicit negative: no named broker or underwriter has published a percentage-of-hull figure dated 22–26 August, and Marsh at 7.5–10% of hull, dated 22 July, remains the newest sourced point estimate; a “5 to 10 percent” figure circulating on 24 August has no named broker and is not used, and straits.live’s multiples are its own editorial estimates rather than market quotes. The Joint War Committee has issued no update; the latest is JWLA-034 of 29 July. On European gas, a named and dated attribution for the 21–25 August move could NOT be sourced to a named analyst at a named bank or consultancy — the only dated attributions retrievable are commodity-desk notes of 24 and 25 August naming the Bessent sanctions package, delayed Qatari LNG deliveries and heat-driven cooling demand, and they are reported as desk notes rather than as analyst calls. European storage stood at 62.99% on 24 August, 17.27 points below the five-year average and the lowest for the date since records began in 2011 — but that is a TASS calculation on GIE data and gie.eu/agsi could not be read directly, so it is Tier 2 pending verification. No new Norwegian outage or extension is dated 22–26 August and Gassco’s own feed was NOT OBTAINED; no QatarEnergy statement is dated in the window.

channels.name: Maritime denial
channels.rationale: Day 180. Update 089 (ICOD 251500 UTC) takes the cumulative confirmed incident count from 94 to 96 on Warnings 119-26 and 120-26, both 24 August; Hormuz remains SEVERE and the environment is still described as an established post-MoU status quo. The Gulf of Oman was CUT from SUBSTANTIAL to MODERATE — the first threat-level reduction this monitor has recorded, and a reclassification of the Musandam strikes into the Hormuz bucket rather than a de-escalation. On 24 August the annex recorded 1 cargo vessel and 0 tankers, Kpler 2 commodity vessels and Windward 4 transits with ZERO OUTBOUND. Blockade tally 71 redirected.

channels.name: Oil price shock
channels.rationale: Brent closed $87.27 on 25 August after two consecutive down-closes from $92.67, and printed $85.31 intraday. The upgrade is $7.73 away on the scored CO2 series and $6.42 on the active close — WIDENED from $3.03 and $1.22, the first widening after four narrowings on a six-reading sequence. The downgrade price leg is $14.79 away and also moved further off. The proximate driver was the Iran–Oman corridor headline, not any change in supply.
channels.move: held — but the gap WIDENED, and this is still the only channel that can move the score UP

channels.name: US inflation impulse
channels.rationale: The 5y5y forward closed 2.2991%, BELOW the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel to 5 on 31 July — the second such close in the current regime and not confirmed by a second close. The documented downgrade at the 2.142% anchor is 15.71 bp lower, narrowed from 20.12, and the rule is NOT moved to match the trigger. BE10 at 2.3135% is just 5.66 bp above its own anchor, from 9.56 bp on 20 August.

channels.name: Treasury stress
channels.rationale: THE TWO DOWNGRADE LEGS CONVERGED FOR THE FIRST TIME, on the 25 August close. MOVE closed 71.92, a sixth consecutive close below 75 and the longest run since 10 June–10 July, while the 30-year gap narrowed 27.09 → 22.45 → 16.51 bp, the narrowest since 28 July. Be exact about 24 August: MOVE rose that day, so it is still rotation; 25 August is the convergence. The yield leg still fails and hysteresis requires sustained, so the channel holds — but this is the live downgrade candidate of the document.
channels.move: held (at max) — the nearest any channel is to a downgrade

channels.name: Political stress
channels.rationale: AUTMUSAG reads $4.82 for a fourth consecutive date and the 24 August value is UNRESOLVED under the field-level rule; the $4.60 condition is 22 cents away, unchanged. The direct reads say the pump is flat to lower — AAA regular FELL to $4.0969 on 25 August, below both its 20 August level and its month-ago level. The shock is in distillate: AAA diesel set a new war high of $5.6199, 19.60 cents from its all-time record, and the EIA weekly rose 19.8 cents after 19.7.

channels.name: Escalation risk
channels.rationale: The strongest downgrade case of the war, and it is still declined. For it: a written Iran–Oman framework naming a corridor and joint demining, a live Pakistani channel, three Gulf capitals pushing toward de-escalation, no strike inside Iran across the window and a 28-day CENTCOM combat silence. Against it: an announcement is not an event — talks have not convened and none are scheduled; Araghchi says the framework does not open the strait; a tanker was DISABLED in Omani waters on 24 August; and Iran legislated toward transit fees and blacklisted 45 or 46 vessels.

2026-08-26.scoreTotal: CRISIS band — HELD, twelfth consecutive edition. FIVE of six channels are pinned at the top of the scale and the sixth, oil, sits three points below it, so deterioration cannot raise this number through any of the five and the sole remaining route up is oil — which moved AWAY from its upgrade this week. The composition to read is the dissonance: the diplomatic record improved materially while the physical strait recorded its thinnest traffic since early May, and the oil price traded the first and ignored the second. Movement inside the frozen total is visible only in the distance-to-trigger figures, which is why they are reported in basis points and dollars every edition.

whatsChanged.title: 4 · What has changed since the 21 August edition
items: Iran and Oman ISSUED a joint statement in Tehran on 25 August naming a temporary joint maritime corridor, a joint mine-clearance project and a technical track to a permanent corridor. It is a framework, not a declaration and not a reopening — Araghchi conditions reopening on US compliance with the memorandum that lapsed on 17 August, and Busaidi cites that lapsed document’s Article 5 as the corridor’s legal basis. No signature or signatory is recorded anywhere, which is why this document says ISSUED rather than signed.

The oil rally gave back most of itself in two closes — $92.67 to $90.54 to $87.27, and $85.31 intraday. The edition-over-edition upgrade gap widened from $3.03 to $7.73 on the scored series and from $1.22 to $6.42 on the active, the first widening after four narrowings. On the intervening closes the gap actually reached $2.33 on 21 August before widening, so the true low was $2.33 and the widening began on 24 August.

The strait got THINNER while the price fell. One cargo vessel and no tankers on the UKMTO annex for 24 August; Kpler two commodity vessels, its thinnest day since early May; Windward four transits and NOT ONE OUTBOUND. Update 089 moves the incident count from 94 to 96 and the blockade tally from 65 to 71 redirected.

Stage-4 Threshold B LAPSED on the 25 August close, on both legs at once — the 30-year short by 3.49 bp and the 10-year by 2.12. The fifth arming lasted three closes. This is the sixth lapse, the eleventh state and the tenth change since 29 July, and it corrects the standing count to EIGHT of the previous NINE states lasting three closes or fewer.

THE TREASURY DOWNGRADE LEGS CONVERGED FOR THE FIRST TIME. MOVE closed below 75 for a sixth consecutive session, its longest run since 10 June–10 July, while the 30-year gap narrowed to 16.51 bp, the narrowest since 28 July. The standing observation since 6 August that these legs rotate rather than converge no longer fits the data — though 24 August was still rotation, because MOVE rose that day.

Washington escalated economically on 24 August and withheld its heaviest instrument. “Operation Economic Outcast”: roughly 60 designations and five NEW E.O. 13902 sector determinations across aviation, digital assets, gold, shipping and technology — but no Chinese teapot refinery, no Chinese port, no Chinese bank, no new Iranian bank and no new executive order. Bessent set a countdown instead and signalled a financial-institution designation “before end of week”.

The Gulf moved the opposite way within 24 hours. Saudi Arabia, with Macron, called for navigation to return to its “normal state” and opposed “any direct or indirect tolls”; Qatar said officials are on the phone “on a daily basis” to restart talks and noted the sanctions are not UN sanctions; and Gargash called for “a political way out of the war”. The coalition is not following the rhetoric. Pakistan’s Field Marshal Munir spent 24 August in Tehran with reopening on the agenda.

Diesel decoupled from gasoline. AAA diesel reached $5.6199 on 25 August, a new war high 19.60 cents from the all-time record, and the EIA weekly on-highway series rose 19.8 cents after 19.7 — two consecutive weeks of nearly twenty cents. Meanwhile the scored AUTMUSAG all-grades series did not move at all and AAA’s regular headline FELL to $4.0969, below both its 20 August level and its month-ago level.

Both gas benchmarks set fresh records. TTF took a new war-record close of €68.320 on 24 August, its third record close in three sessions and the first above €68, and Asia LNG set a new war high of ¥3,793 on 25 August, its third consecutive record — while Henry Hub closed 9.57% BELOW its pre-war anchor in the same week.

Trump declared the Strait mine-free on 25 August, citing the Navy, with a “Zero Tolerance policy” — and UKMTO Update 089, published the same day, states that mine danger areas remain ACTIVE in and adjacent to the TSS. Both are reported and neither is reconciled. A tanker was DISABLED by a projectile in Omani waters roughly twenty-four hours before the declaration.

The field-level exact-equality rule was vindicated a THIRD time. The 21 August 30-year, published UNRESOLVED because it printed identical to four decimals to the 20 August close, settles in this extract at 5.2709% — a genuine 2.33 bp rise. It also fired twice prospectively, on SOFR and AUTMUSAG in the 24 August row, and the basis check cleared on both oil contracts.

A LONG-STANDING BUILD DEFECT WAS FOUND AND FIXED. The PDF build was passing table column widths as raw numbers, which the renderer reads as points rather than millimetres, so every table since the 21 August format change had been rendering at roughly a third of its intended width. Three text QA passes missed it and the visual render caught it. The edition is 6 pages and the annex 7 as a result, rather than the 9 the bug had forced.

scenarios.name: Deal collapse — talks stall on terms
scenarios.desc: Modal for a ninth consecutive edition. The strait stays shut not because talks failed to start but because the terms are irreconcilable: Iran demands sanctions relief, released assets, an end to the blockade and a halt to operations on all fronts; the US demands restored free passage, no nuclear weapons and no proxy funding, and is running a blockade to compel it.
scenarios.shift: –1 (44 → 43). A written framework naming a corridor and a joint demining project now exists, which lowers the odds of pure collapse at the margin. Held to one point because it is an Oman–Iran instrument rather than a US–Iran one, because it is legally anchored to a memorandum that lapsed on 17 August, and because Araghchi conditioned reopening on US compliance with that dead document the same day he announced it.

scenarios.name: Return to full war
scenarios.desc: Sustained US or Israeli strikes inside Iran resume, or Iran strikes US regional bases or Gulf states directly.
scenarios.shift: –3 (23 → 20), a second consecutive reduction and the largest single cut in this cell since 17 August. Two NON-COMPARABLE clocks, both long, and they are not to be conflated: a 26-night run with no strike inside Iran, dated from the 1 August cancellation, and a 28-day CENTCOM press silence on combat inside Iran, dated from the 29 July release. Add a US posture that has explicitly substituted economic for kinetic pressure — Hegseth on 24 August: “Economic pressure is what we know hurts them the most.” Against it: Rezaei’s nuclear remark, which is single-stream Tier 2 of Tier 3 material and is not used to move this cell.

scenarios.name: Contained but violent
scenarios.desc: Attacks continue on shipping and on Gulf energy infrastructure; the blockade persists; neither side crosses into sustained state-on-state strikes.
scenarios.shift: +1 (21 → 22). A tanker was DISABLED by a projectile in Omani waters on 24 August, the blockade tally moved from 65 to 71, and UKMTO’s own assessment language still describes an established post-MoU status quo rather than an escalation. A steady rate of attacks against a functioning blockade and an unchanged Hormuz threat level is the definition of this cell, and the provider is still naming it.

scenarios.name: Regional relapse
scenarios.desc: The conflict widens through the Red Sea, Lebanon, Iraq or the Saudi energy complex rather than through the strait itself.
scenarios.shift: Unchanged (9), and deliberately so. Arguing up: Rezaei named Saudi and Emirati bypass pipeline routes as within the target set on 24 August, and a Houthi missile struck the Saudi VLCC AMZAN off Yanbu the same day. Arguing for restraint: the Rezaei statement is Tier 2 reporting of Tier 3 source material, single-stream, with no Tier 1 wire pickup located, and this document does not move a probability on it; the Yanbu strike left the vessel making way under her own power. The cell holds on standing structural risk rather than on either item.

scenarios.name: Mediated pause
scenarios.desc: A negotiated de-escalation restores partial transit under a supervised regime.
scenarios.shift: +3 (3 → 6) — its FIRST rise since 17 August and off the record low. Justified by an ISSUED joint statement that NAMES a temporary corridor and a joint mine-clearance project, by a live Pakistani channel that carried a reopening agenda into Tehran on 24 August, and by three Gulf capitals pushing publicly toward de-escalation. NOT justified by a project that yet exists, and NOT by talks: US–Iran negotiations have not resumed and none are scheduled, and the framework’s own Iranian principal says it does not open the strait. Three points is the largest single move this cell has made and it is still only six.

2026-08-26.scenarioShift: Probabilities sum to 100. Shifts from the 21 Aug edition: deal collapse –1 (44 → 43) on the existence of a written framework; full war –3 (23 → 20) on 26 nights without a strike inside Iran, a 28-day CENTCOM press silence and a posture that has substituted economic for kinetic pressure; contained-but-violent +1 (21 → 22) on a tanker disabled in Omani waters and UKMTO’s own status-quo language; regional relapse unchanged at 9; mediated pause +3 (3 → 6), its first rise since 17 August. DEAL COLLAPSE AND FULL WAR NOW CARRY 63% BETWEEN THEM, DOWN FROM 67% — the first fall in that pair since 17 August. Note that 63% is NOT a label for “the strait stays shut”: four of the five scenarios keep it shut, and only the mediated pause at 6% reopens it.
watchlist: Whether the Treasury downgrade legs stay converged. A 30-year close below 5.00% with MOVE still under 75 is the market-channel downgrade whose both legs are now moving together — 16.51 bp on the close, 17.34 intraday, with the volatility leg six sessions old. Note that the US-inflation leg is numerically nearer at 15.71 bp, but it sits on a forward that has twice broken and retraced within a session, which is why the Treasury leg is the more durable candidate. Hysteresis requires sustained; do not move either channel on one close.

Whether Threshold B re-arms on the 26 August close. The margins are 2.66 bp on the 30-year and 1.33 bp on the 10-year, both inside a single session’s range. That would be the fourth one-session round trip of the war, after 10, 14 and 20 August.

Whether the Iran–Oman corridor is actually announced. Busaidi said “soon” on 25 August. Watch fm.gov.om and the Oman News Agency for route coordinates — coordinates, not communiqués, are the test. No US–Iran talks are scheduled and that remains the gate on everything else.

Whether Bessent’s threatened financial-institution designation issues. He signalled one “before end of week”, which lands on top of Warsh’s Friday keynote. Watch OFAC recent actions and the Federal Register, and specifically whether it reaches a Chinese bank — which the 24 August package deliberately did not.

Whether the mine claim survives contact with the next advisory. Trump declared the Strait mine-free on 25 August and UKMTO Update 089, the same day, says mine danger areas remain active in and adjacent to the TSS. Update 090 and VRA Overview No. 4 settle it. Fetch by DIRECT FILE URL — the product indexes render empty to a fetcher.

Whether Brent stabilises or keeps giving back the rally. Two down closes and $85.31 intraday. Quote both bases every time, and watch the 26 August EIA weekly — not obtained at the cut — for the crude imports line and for whether the SPR drew again from 293.4 mn bbl.

Whether diesel takes out $5.8159. AAA is 19.60 cents away after 15.22 cents in a week, and the EIA weekly has now posted two consecutive rises of nearly twenty cents. It is not the scored series and cannot move the political channel — say so — but an all-time high in freight fuel is the shock arriving where the scored series cannot see it.

Whether CENTCOM’s combat silence breaks at 28 days, and whether the George Washington strike group entering the Gulf of Oman or the Gulf changes the operational tempo. It is currently in the Arabian Sea and has not entered either.

Whether the UAE ever publishes an implementing decree, carve-out or licence regime for the embargo it announced on 19 August. Eight days on there is nothing, which is itself the test of how binding the measure is.

Whether Jackson Hole produces anything on the energy shock. The 2026 theme is payments and financial innovation, so any signal will come outside the formal programme — in the framing of Warsh’s first keynote at 10:00 ET on Friday 28 August, or in sideline press.

protocol.step: Score on confirmed closes, with hysteresis, and QA in three passes
protocol.detail: Never move a market channel on an intraday print; never whipsaw on a single session; never move a downgrade rule to match the level that fired the upgrade. Then run three QA passes, in order: a numeric harness recomputing every figure against the dataframe; an adversarial PROSE pass by a reviewer with no access to the source data, run TWICE because the fixing introduces its own defects; and a VISUAL render.
